group.title: Health and wellbeing
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: A substance in food that the body needs to grow and stay healthy.
examples: Spinach is full of {nutrients} like iron.
wrong: A nutrient is a harmful substance with no use to the body.

words.meaning: The chemical processes in the body that turn food into energy.
examples: Exercise can speed up your {metabolism}.
wrong: Metabolism is the name of a bone in the arm.

words.meaning: Involving a lot of sitting and little physical activity.
examples: Office workers often have {sedentary} lifestyles.
wrong: His sedentary job keeps him running all day.

words.meaning: Good for your health or morally good.
examples: She cooks simple, {wholesome} meals.
wrong: The wholesome meal was full of junk and sugar.

words.meaning: Calmly paying full attention to the present moment.
examples: Ten minutes of {mindfulness} each morning helps me focus.
wrong: Mindfulness means worrying about the future all day.

words.meaning: A fixed plan of diet, exercise or treatment that you follow.
examples: His daily {regimen} includes a run and a cold shower.
wrong: A regimen is a plan you change randomly every hour.

words.meaning: The way you hold your body when standing or sitting.
examples: Sitting up straight improves your {posture}.
wrong: Good posture means slouching over your desk all day.

words.meaning: Taking in enough water for the body to work well.
examples: Good {hydration} matters most on hot days.
wrong: For better hydration, drink as little water as possible.

words.meaning: Lacking enough water in the body.
examples: Drink more water or you’ll get {dehydrated}.
wrong: He was dehydrated after drinking five liters of water.

words.meaning: Connected with the heart and blood vessels.
examples: Swimming is great for {cardiovascular} health.
wrong: Cardiovascular disease affects only the hair.

words.meaning: The energy and strength to keep going for a long time.
examples: Marathon runners need great {stamina}.
wrong: With his stamina, he was tired after ten steps.

words.meaning: Keeping within sensible limits, not having too much.
examples: You can eat sweets in {moderation}.
wrong: Eating in moderation means having as much as you can.

words.meaning: A fatty substance in the blood; too much can harm the heart.
examples: Fried food can raise your {cholesterol}.
wrong: Cholesterol is a vitamin found only in fresh fruit.

words.meaning: A popular eating plan that promises quick weight loss but rarely lasts.
examples: The cabbage soup {fad diet} was popular for one summer.
wrong: A fad diet is a balanced eating plan doctors trust for life.

words.meaning: A poisonous substance, often made by a plant or living thing.
examples: Some mushrooms contain deadly {toxins}.
wrong: Toxins are vitamins that keep the body healthy.

words.meaning: Meant to stop illness or problems before they happen.
examples: Regular checkups are a form of {preventive} care.
wrong: Preventive medicine is given only after the illness is serious.

words.meaning: Poor health caused by not eating enough or the right kinds of food.
examples: Many children in the camp suffered from {malnutrition}.
wrong: His malnutrition came from eating a perfect, varied diet.

words.meaning: To get back your health and strength after illness or effort.
examples: She went to the coast to {recuperate} after surgery.
wrong: He recuperated by working day and night without sleep.

words.meaning: To make someone feel or look young and full of energy again.
examples: A week in the mountains {rejuvenated} me.
wrong: The rest rejuvenated her, so she felt old and drained.

words.meaning: Making you feel healthy and full of energy.
examples: We took an {invigorating} swim in the cold lake.
wrong: The invigorating walk left him weak and sleepy.

words.meaning: Helping you feel better or heal.
examples: Gardening can be very {therapeutic}.
wrong: The therapeutic massage made her pain much worse.

words.meaning: A period of avoiding harmful things, such as junk food or screens.
examples: I’m on a digital {detox} this weekend, no phone at all.
wrong: During his phone detox, he checked his phone every minute.

words.meaning: Things you do to look after your own health and happiness.
examples: A long bath is my favorite kind of {self-care}.
wrong: Self-care means ignoring your own needs completely.

words.meaning: A healthy split of time between your job and your private life.
examples: Working every weekend ruined his {work-life balance}.
wrong: She has a great work-life balance, so she never sees her family.

words.meaning: To relax after a period of work or stress.
examples: I like to {unwind} with a book after work.
wrong: He unwound by taking on three extra projects.

words.meaning: A minor illness.
examples: Colds and headaches are common {ailments}.
wrong: An ailment is a medal for good health.

words.meaning: Great energy and liveliness.
examples: At eighty, she is still full of {vitality}.
wrong: His vitality made him dull and lifeless.

words.meaning: Weak and thin, often because of old age or illness.
examples: Her grandfather is too {frail} to climb stairs.
wrong: The frail old man lifted the heavy piano alone.

words.meaning: Systems that keep places clean, such as clean water and drains.
examples: Poor {sanitation} spreads disease.
wrong: Good sanitation means letting dirty water run in the streets.

words.meaning: To have too much of something you enjoy, such as food or drink.
examples: It’s easy to {overindulge} during the holidays.
wrong: She overindulged by eating a single grape.

words.meaning: Helping to bring back your health, strength or energy.
examples: Deep sleep has a {restorative} effect.
wrong: The restorative break left everyone more worn out.

words.meaning: Not getting enough rest at night over a period of time.
examples: {Sleep deprivation} makes it hard to concentrate.
wrong: Sleep deprivation is caused by sleeping ten hours a night.

words.meaning: Meals and snacks changed in factories, often with added salt, sugar or fat.
examples: Try to cut down on {processed food} like chips and sausages.
wrong: Processed food is fruit picked fresh from the tree.

words.meaning: The shape and size of a person’s body.
examples: Years of swimming gave him a strong {physique}.
wrong: Physique is a person’s sense of humor.

words.meaning: The body’s ability to resist a disease.
examples: Vaccines give you {immunity} to some diseases.
wrong: Strong immunity means you catch every cold going.

words.meaning: Easily affected or harmed by something, such as an illness.
examples: Older people are more {susceptible} to flu.
wrong: Being susceptible to colds means you never catch them.

words.meaning: A lack of something the body needs.
examples: A vitamin D {deficiency} can make you tired.
wrong: An iron deficiency means you have far too much iron.

words.meaning: To rest and slowly get well after a serious illness.
examples: She spent a month {convalescing} at her sister’s house.
wrong: He convalesced by running a marathon the day after surgery.

words.meaning: Lacking energy and not wanting to do anything.
examples: The heat made everyone {lethargic}.
wrong: Feeling lethargic, she ran ten miles with great energy.

words.meaning: Long life.
examples: Diet and exercise both play a part in {longevity}.
wrong: His longevity meant he died very young.
